newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma junta-Suu Kyi dialogue seen as pipedream.
newsitem.headline: Burma junta-Suu Kyi dialogue seen as pipedream.

text.p: Dialogue between Burma's military government and pro-democracy opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi looks unlikely in the near future as both sides adamantly refuse to make the first move, political analysts said.

The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) was now preoccupied with keeping anti-government elements such as restless students, the clergy and Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party (NLD) under control, they said on Thursday.
The SLORC was also busy consolidating recent ceasefires with ethnic guerrilla groups and its 20 members might not agree on how to handle the issue of dialogue, they added.

The SLORC, which closed universities after December anti-government street protests by thousands of students, has still not said when it will reopen them and has parked tanks in strategic places in Rangoon as a show of force.

For her part, Suu Kyi has adopted a confrontational approach to the SLORC because it has restricted her movements, harassed the NLD at the grassroots and refused to recognise it as the rightful winner of a 1990 general election, they said.
"It is a question of face and what is at stake. Neither side wants to give in and the question of dialogue looks unlikely for now," said an Asian diplomat.

Suu Kyi angered the SLORC in November 1995 when she abruptly withdrew her NLD from the government-appointed National Convention charged with writing Burma's new constitution. She was released from six years of house arrest in July that year.
She called the convention a sham and demanded that the SLORC immediately restore more democracy and freedom in the country. The West supported her, further angering Rangoon.
SLORC spokesmen insist the convention is the only forum that must shape any future government or system for Burma.
"She left the convention against the rules. Why should we ask her to come back? It's against rules," a spokesman said.

But some western diplomats felt otherwise. "It's the government which holds the power and they have the power to resolve the problem. They must start the issue. She (Suu Kyi) can't make it happen," said one.
The last time the national convention met was in April 1996.

The government spokesman said any delay in reconvening the convention was due to the time it took to reach consensus with ethnic groups on key issues. But Suu Kyi and some diplomats believed the delay in reconvening could be a tactic by the SLORC to remain in power longer.
They also speculated that army hardliners within the SLORC, whose hallmark is collective decision-making, might be refusing to hold any dialogue.
SLORC founding member Lieutenant General Kyaw Ba on Monday bluntly ruled out any dialogue with Suu Kyi and also denied talk of any rift within the ruling junta.
"She will always be against us...at this time it is impossible," Kyaw Ba, who is also hotels and tourism minister, told Reuters in an interview.
On rumours of a SLORC division, he said: "We don't have anything like that. We are united. If we have differences, we can easily be destroyed by others."
Statements by two expelled NLD members of parliament that Suu Kyi soften her stance against the SLORC and rejoin the convention was viewed by some as "philosophically sound."

But they said the two expelled MPs and their ideas might never become a major third force in the SLORC-Suu Kyi equation because the SLORC would never allow new political parties and Suu Kyi was too popular to defeat at grassroots levels.
The duo, Than Tun and Thein Kyi, were expelled by the NLD for violating party rules while pushing for their ideas.
